claim: Tissue and organ loss to trauma, disease, and physical injury account for approximately $400 billion in annual medical burden.
source: Tissue and organ loss to trauma, disease, and physical injury account for a large proportion of human ailments and approximately $400 billion in annual medical burden (Vela et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vela et al., 2020.

claim: Static cold storage is the standard of care for organ and tissue preservation.
source: This is currently accomplished clinically by lowering temperature and static cold storage is the standard of care for organ and tissue preservation; however, its long-term use can cause damage to the integrity of the graft (Vela et al., 2020; Petrenko et al., 2019; Guibert et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vela et al., 2020; Petrenko et al., 2019; Guibert et al., 2011.

claim: Long-term use of static cold storage can cause damage to the integrity of the graft.
source: This is currently accomplished clinically by lowering temperature and static cold storage is the standard of care for organ and tissue preservation; however, its long-term use can cause damage to the integrity of the graft (Vela et al., 2020; Petrenko et al., 2019; Guibert et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vela et al., 2020; Petrenko et al., 2019; Guibert et al., 2011.

claim: Hypothermia has been used to induce a state of biostasis clinically using ex vivo machine perfusion technologies during cardiac transplant surgery.
source: Hypothermia has also been used to induce a state of biostasis clinically using ex vivo machine perfusion technologies, e.g., during cardiac transplant surgery.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical practice.

claim: Combination of protective agents with perfusion and/or partial freezing approaches have extended preservation times in rat livers and whole pigs.
source: Combination of protective agents with perfusion and/or partial freezing approaches have extended preservation times in rat livers and whole pigs (Andrijevic et al., 2022; Tessier et al., 2022), and neural modulation approaches have been successful at demonstrating central control of body temperature and general metabolic state (Hrvatin et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Andrijevic et al., 2022; Tessier et al., 2022.

claim: Neural modulation approaches have been successful at demonstrating central control of body temperature and general metabolic state.
source: Combination of protective agents with perfusion and/or partial freezing approaches have extended preservation times in rat livers and whole pigs (Andrijevic et al., 2022; Tessier et al., 2022), and neural modulation approaches have been successful at demonstrating central control of body temperature and general metabolic state (Hrvatin et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hrvatin et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2020.

claim: H2S exposure has been reported to induce a hypometabolic state in a rodent model.
source: H2S exposure has been reported to induce a hypometabolic state (reduced metabolism and body temperature) in a rodent model, although this was later found to be mediated in part by a low baseline laboratory temperature (Blackstone et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blackstone et al., 1979.

claim: The hypometabolic state induced by H2S exposure in rodents was later found to be mediated in part by a low baseline laboratory temperature.
source: H2S exposure has been reported to induce a hypometabolic state (reduced metabolism and body temperature) in a rodent model, although this was later found to be mediated in part by a low baseline laboratory temperature (Blackstone et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blackstone et al., 1979.

claim: The synthetic opioid peptide DADLE can induce hypometabolism and improve organ preservation via a delta opioid receptor mechanism.
source: The synthetic opioid peptide DADLE can also induce hypometabolism and improve organ preservation via a delta opioid receptor (DOR) mechanism, but with varied results (Beal et al., 2019; Ratigan and McKay, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beal et al., 2019; Ratigan and McKay, 2016.

claim: SNC80 has been shown to induce hypothermia in rodents.
source: This drug caught our attention because it has been shown to induce hypothermia and protect against the effects of spinal cord ischemia in rodents (Rawls et al., 2005; Horiuchi et al., 2004), however, further study was required to understand if these observations were related to biostatic effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rawls et al., 2005; Horiuchi et al., 2004.

claim: SNC80 has been shown to protect against the effects of spinal cord ischemia in rodents.
source: This drug caught our attention because it has been shown to induce hypothermia and protect against the effects of spinal cord ischemia in rodents (Rawls et al., 2005; Horiuchi et al., 2004), however, further study was required to understand if these observations were related to biostatic effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rawls et al., 2005; Horiuchi et al., 2004.

claim: 100 μM SNC80 slows movement in mobile Xenopus tadpoles, reducing activity by approximately 50% within 1 hr.
source: Behavioral assessment in mobile tadpoles showed that 100 μM SNC80 slows movement relative to vehicle-treated counterparts, reducing activity by approximately 50% within 1 hr, which is rapidly reversible when the drug is removed (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The movement slowing effect of SNC80 in Xenopus tadpoles is rapidly reversible when the drug is removed.
source: Behavioral assessment in mobile tadpoles showed that 100 μM SNC80 slows movement relative to vehicle-treated counterparts, reducing activity by approximately 50% within 1 hr, which is rapidly reversible when the drug is removed (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: SNC80 suppressed the rate of oxygen consumption to one-third of baseline within 3 hr of treatment in Xenopus tadpoles.
source: SNC80 also suppressed the rate of oxygen consumption to one-third of baseline within 3 hr of treatment (Figure 1b) and had extreme suppressive, but fully reversible, effects on heart rate after only 1 hr of exposure (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SNC80 had extreme suppressive, but fully reversible, effects on heart rate in Xenopus tadpoles after only 1 hr of exposure.
source: SNC80 also suppressed the rate of oxygen consumption to one-third of baseline within 3 hr of treatment (Figure 1b) and had extreme suppressive, but fully reversible, effects on heart rate after only 1 hr of exposure (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Oxygen consumption was reduced in immobile Xenopus embryos treated with SNC80.
source: Oxygen consumption was reduced in immobile Xenopus embryos treated with SNC80 as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that its metabolism-suppressing effects are independent of the slowed movement observed in mobile tadpoles.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The metabolism-suppressing effects of SNC80 are independent of the slowed movement observed in mobile tadpoles.
source: Oxygen consumption was reduced in immobile Xenopus embryos treated with SNC80 as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that its metabolism-suppressing effects are independent of the slowed movement observed in mobile tadpoles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that immobile embryos also show reduced oxygen consumption.

claim: SNC80 was detected within 1 hr of treatment in Xenopus tadpoles.
source: SNC80 was detected within 1 hr of treatment and it appeared in a punctate distribution in the gastrointestinal tract, gill region, and skeletal muscle (Figure 2a and b), suggesting full-body delivery of the drug.
evidence: The claim is supported by MALDI-ToF MSI data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: SNC80 appeared in a punctate distribution in the gastrointestinal tract, gill region, and skeletal muscle of Xenopus tadpoles.
source: SNC80 was detected within 1 hr of treatment and it appeared in a punctate distribution in the gastrointestinal tract, gill region, and skeletal muscle (Figure 2a and b), suggesting full-body delivery of the drug.
evidence: The claim is supported by MALDI-ToF MSI data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: The distribution of SNC80 in Xenopus tadpoles suggests full-body delivery of the drug.
source: SNC80 was detected within 1 hr of treatment and it appeared in a punctate distribution in the gastrointestinal tract, gill region, and skeletal muscle (Figure 2a and b), suggesting full-body delivery of the drug.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the distribution pattern observed in MALDI-ToF MSI data.

claim: MALDI-ToF MSI analysis revealed significantly higher levels of acylcarnitine and cholesterol ester in SNC80-treated Xenopus in both skeletal muscle and brain, but not in cardiac tissue.
source: Similarly, MALDI-ToF MSI analysis revealed significantly higher levels of acylcarnitine and cholesterol ester in SNC80-treated groups in both skeletal muscle and brain, but not in cardiac tissue (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by MALDI-ToF MSI data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Increased levels of long chain acylcarnitine associated with enhanced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation are observed during fasting as well as in hibernating brown bears.
source: Increased levels of long chain acylcarnitine associated with enhanced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation are observed during fasting as well as in hibernating brown bears (Soeters et al., 2009; Welinder et al., 2016), and cholesterol ester levels increase in hibernating ground squirrels (Otis et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Soeters et al., 2009; Welinder et al., 2016.

claim: Cholesterol ester levels increase in hibernating ground squirrels.
source: Increased levels of long chain acylcarnitine associated with enhanced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation are observed during fasting as well as in hibernating brown bears (Soeters et al., 2009; Welinder et al., 2016), and cholesterol ester levels increase in hibernating ground squirrels (Otis et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Otis et al., 2011.

claim: The DOR antagonist naltrindole at 200 μM did not block the hypometabolic effects of 100 μM SNC80 in Xenopus tadpoles.
source: However, when we tested the DOR antagonist, naltrindole (NTI), at double the concentration (200 μM) relative to SNC80 (100 μM), it did not block the hypometabolic effects of SNC80 (Figure 2d), suggesting that SNC80 modulates metabolism independent of DOR activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: SNC80 modulates metabolism independent of DOR activation.
source: However, when we tested the DOR antagonist, naltrindole (NTI), at double the concentration (200 μM) relative to SNC80 (100 μM), it did not block the hypometabolic effects of SNC80 (Figure 2d), suggesting that SNC80 modulates metabolism independent of DOR activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that naltrindole did not block SNC80's effects.

claim: WB3 exhibited an IC50 of 3470 nM for DOR binding.
source: A specific binding curve could not be fit for SNC80 due to its high affinity and therefore its IC50 is <4.6 nM, whereas WB3 exhibited an IC50 of 3470 nM (Figure 3b), suggesting almost 1000 times less DOR binding activity for WB3 compared to SNC80.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioligand binding assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: SNC80 has an IC50 of <4.6 nM for DOR binding.
source: A specific binding curve could not be fit for SNC80 due to its high affinity and therefore its IC50 is <4.6 nM, whereas WB3 exhibited an IC50 of 3470 nM (Figure 3b), suggesting almost 1000 times less DOR binding activity for WB3 compared to SNC80.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioligand binding assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: WB3 has almost 1000 times less DOR binding activity compared to SNC80.
source: A specific binding curve could not be fit for SNC80 due to its high affinity and therefore its IC50 is <4.6 nM, whereas WB3 exhibited an IC50 of 3470 nM (Figure 3b), suggesting almost 1000 times less DOR binding activity for WB3 compared to SNC80.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the IC50 values measured for SNC80 and WB3.

claim: WB3 retains physiological slowing properties in vivo despite lacking delta opioid activity.
source: Subsequently, we screened WB3 in the Xenopus swimming, oxygen consumption, and heart rate assays and found that the analog retains physiological slowing properties in vivo despite lacking delta opioid activity (Figure 3c, d, and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c, d, and e.

claim: More potent and rapid effects on swimming were observed with exposure to WB3 compared to SNC80 in Xenopus tadpoles.
source: In fact, we observed more potent and rapid effects on swimming with exposure to WB3 compared to SNC80, suggesting that the non-opioid properties of SNC80 may be primarily responsible for its observed physiological effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing WB3 and SNC80.

claim: The non-opioid properties of SNC80 may be primarily responsible for its observed physiological effects.
source: In fact, we observed more potent and rapid effects on swimming with exposure to WB3 compared to SNC80, suggesting that the non-opioid properties of SNC80 may be primarily responsible for its observed physiological effects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that WB3, with reduced DOR activity, has more potent effects.

claim: Hearts are currently allocated to patients located within 4 hr of organ removal from the donor.
source: Currently, hearts are allocated to patients located within 4 hr of organ removal from the donor.
evidence: The claim is stated as current clinical practice.

claim: Prior work has demonstrated that the VP.S ENCORE enhances cardiac viability over standard of care-static cold storage.
source: Prior work has demonstrated that the VP.S ENCORE enhances cardiac viability over standard of care-static cold storage and hearts perfused in this device for 4 hr demonstrate similar cardiac function to a healthy heart in both preclinical animal models and human deceased donor hearts (Veraza et al., 2023; Andrijauskaite et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veraza et al., 2023; Andrijauskaite et al., 2023.

claim: Hearts perfused in the VP.S ENCORE device for 4 hr demonstrate similar cardiac function to a healthy heart in both preclinical animal models and human deceased donor hearts.
source: Prior work has demonstrated that the VP.S ENCORE enhances cardiac viability over standard of care-static cold storage and hearts perfused in this device for 4 hr demonstrate similar cardiac function to a healthy heart in both preclinical animal models and human deceased donor hearts (Veraza et al., 2023; Andrijauskaite et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veraza et al., 2023; Andrijauskaite et al., 2023.

claim: With SNC80 treatment, a rapid decline in the heart's oxygen consumption to <50% of that observed in hearts exposed to the vehicle control was observed, which was sustained over the 6 hr preservation period.
source: Importantly, with SNC80 treatment, we observed a rapid decline in the heart's oxygen consumption to <50% of that observed in hearts exposed to the vehicle control, which was sustained over the 6 hr preservation period (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: After 30 min of reperfusion and before defibrillation, SNC80-treated hearts had a lower oxygen consumption level than vehicle-treated hearts (2.39 ± 1.23 versus 4.28 ± 2.48 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at the 30 min timepoint).
source: After 30 min of reperfusion and before defibrillation, SNC80-treated hearts had a lower oxygen consumption level than vehicle-treated hearts (2.39 ± 1.23 versus 4.28 ± 2.48 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at the 30 min timepoint) (Figure 4b) that recovered to normal levels after defibrillation and with increases in temperature (2.49 ± 0.53 and 2.35 ± 0.31 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at 60 min post defibrillation) (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Oxygen consumption in SNC80-treated hearts recovered to normal levels after defibrillation and with increases in temperature (2.49 ± 0.53 and 2.35 ± 0.31 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at 60 min post defibrillation).
source: After 30 min of reperfusion and before defibrillation, SNC80-treated hearts had a lower oxygen consumption level than vehicle-treated hearts (2.39 ± 1.23 versus 4.28 ± 2.48 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at the 30 min timepoint) (Figure 4b) that recovered to normal levels after defibrillation and with increases in temperature (2.49 ± 0.53 and 2.35 ± 0.31 mL/min/100 g, respectively, at 60 min post defibrillation) (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: No evidence of substantial change in LV contractility or relaxation were detected in SNC80-exposed hearts, either before or after they were defibrillated and exposed to epinephrine.
source: No evidence of substantial change in LV contractility or relaxation were detected in SNC80-exposed hearts, either before or after they were defibrillated and exposed to epinephrine (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Gene expression analysis of heart biopsy samples showed significant reduction of markers of inflammation (IL-6, IL-8, TNFα), hypoxia (Hif1α), and cell death (TP53, BCL2) in SNC80-treated hearts when compared to vehicle control hearts.
source: Gene expression analysis of heart biopsy samples showed significant reduction of markers of inflammation (IL-6, IL-8, TNFα), hypoxia (Hif1α), and cell death (TP53, BCL2) in SNC80-treated hearts when compared to vehicle control hearts (Figure 4e), and no changes in the mitochondrial ATP synthase marker, ATP5MC3, were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: No changes in the mitochondrial ATP synthase marker, ATP5MC3, were observed in SNC80-treated hearts compared to vehicle control hearts.
source: Gene expression analysis of heart biopsy samples showed significant reduction of markers of inflammation (IL-6, IL-8, TNFα), hypoxia (Hif1α), and cell death (TP53, BCL2) in SNC80-treated hearts when compared to vehicle control hearts (Figure 4e), and no changes in the mitochondrial ATP synthase marker, ATP5MC3, were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Histopathological evaluation showed retention of normal muscle morphology without signs of tissue edema immediately after perfusion in the VP.S ENCORE in SNC80-treated hearts.
source: Histopathological evaluation showed retention of normal muscle morphology (Figure 4f) without signs of tissue edema immediately after perfusion in the VP.S ENCORE.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In some hearts treated with SNC80 greater waviness of muscle fibers was observed, possibly indicating a state of muscle contraction.
source: In some hearts treated with SNC80 greater waviness of muscle fibers was observed, possibly indicating a state of muscle contraction.
evidence: The claim is based on histological observations and speculation about their meaning.

claim: After defibrillation by electric shock and epinephrine delivery, the P and QRS waveforms were visible in ECGs from three of four SNC80-treated hearts.
source: After defibrillation by electric shock and epinephrine delivery, the P and QRS waveforms were visible in ECGs from three of four SNC80-treated hearts (Supplementary file 1), indicating that those hearts regained atrial and ventricular depolarization (internal charge of cardiac cells become less negative).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The presence of the P and QRS waveforms in SNC80-treated hearts suggests that the intrinsic atrial and ventricular muscle fiber contractility was preserved and the overall conduction system of the heart was viable.
source: The presence of the P and QRS waveforms suggests that the intrinsic atrial and ventricular muscle fiber contractility was preserved and the overall conduction system of the heart was viable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of P and QRS waveforms in ECG data.

claim: The pulse rates of SNC80-treated hearts were at or near normal range for porcine hearts (70–120 beats/min) after defibrillation.
source: The pulse rates of SNC80-treated hearts were at or near normal range for porcine hearts (70–120 beats/min) after defibrillation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG data.

claim: Vehicle-treated hearts exhibited tachycardia following defibrillation, with all exhibiting pulse rates above the normal range for porcine hearts.
source: Vehicle-treated hearts exhibited tachycardia following defibrillation, with all exhibiting pulse rates above the normal range for porcine hearts.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG data.

claim: The relative metabolic rate measured during 3 hr of SNC80 exposure was significantly lower compared to vehicle-treated limbs.
source: Again, we found that the relative metabolic rate measured during 3 hr of SNC80 exposure was significantly lower compared to vehicle-treated limbs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Histopathological evaluation of porcine limbs showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in muscle bundle area.
source: Histopathological evaluation also showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in muscle bundle area (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) or glycogen content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that the tissue's potential for ATP synthesis was not compromised after SNC80 administration, although an increase in intercellular spacing was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Histopathological evaluation of porcine limbs showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in glycogen content.
source: Histopathological evaluation also showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in muscle bundle area (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) or glycogen content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that the tissue's potential for ATP synthesis was not compromised after SNC80 administration, although an increase in intercellular spacing was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The tissue's potential for ATP synthesis was not compromised after SNC80 administration in porcine limbs.
source: Histopathological evaluation also showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in muscle bundle area (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) or glycogen content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that the tissue's potential for ATP synthesis was not compromised after SNC80 administration, although an increase in intercellular spacing was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of retained muscle morphology and glycogen content.

claim: An increase in intercellular spacing was observed in porcine limbs after SNC80 administration.
source: Histopathological evaluation also showed retention of normal muscle morphology with no apparent changes in muscle bundle area (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) or glycogen content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that the tissue's potential for ATP synthesis was not compromised after SNC80 administration, although an increase in intercellular spacing was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: TPP of SNC80-treated Xenopus tissues revealed 19 direct and indirect binding targets.
source: TPP of SNC80-treated Xenopus tissues revealed 19 direct and indirect binding targets (Table 1), including proteins involved in transmembrane transport, mitochondrion activity, and metabolic processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by TPP data shown in Table 1.

claim: Two potentially interesting binding targets of SNC80 are the excitatory amino acid transporter 1 (EAAT1, also known as SLC1A3) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1, also known as SLC8A1).
source: Two potentially interesting binding targets of SNC80 are the excitatory amino acid transporter 1 (EAAT1, also known as SLC1A3) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1, also known as SLC8A1), both of which have been identified in cardiac tissue (Ralphe et al., 2004; Maiolino et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by TPP data and citations to Ralphe et al., 2004; Maiolino et al., 2017.

claim: EAAT1 and NCX1 have been identified in cardiac tissue.
source: Two potentially interesting binding targets of SNC80 are the excitatory amino acid transporter 1 (EAAT1, also known as SLC1A3) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1, also known as SLC8A1), both of which have been identified in cardiac tissue (Ralphe et al., 2004; Maiolino et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ralphe et al., 2004; Maiolino et al., 2017.

claim: Mitochondrial ATP production has been previously reported to be stimulated through intermolecular interactions between EAATs and NCXs in neurons.
source: In addition to their individual functions, mitochondrial ATP production has been previously reported to be stimulated through intermolecular interactions between EAATs and NCXs in neurons (Magi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Magi et al., 2013.

claim: If the EAAT-NCX complex is present in cardiac tissue, inhibition of EAAT and NCX1 could reduce cellular ATP levels.
source: If this complex is also present in cardiac tissue, inhibition of EAAT and NCX1 could reduce cellular ATP levels (Magi et al., 2019), and thereby play a role in slowing metabolism.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to Magi et al., 2019.

claim: The blockade of Na+/Ca2+ exchange via interference with EAAT1-NCX1 interactions could prevent the influx of calcium into the mitochondria that is necessary for calcium-sensitive mitochondrial dehydrogenases that fuel ATP synthesis.
source: Specifically, the blockade of Na+/Ca2+ exchange via interference with EAAT1-NCX1 interactions could prevent the influx of calcium into the mitochondria that is necessary for calcium-sensitive mitochondrial dehydrogenases that fuel ATP synthesis (Magi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to Magi et al., 2019.

claim: TPP identified two additional SNC80-binding proteins located within the mitochondrion: TOMM40 and COX6C.
source: TPP also identified two additional SNC80-binding proteins located within the mitochondrion: TOMM40 and COX6C.
evidence: The claim is supported by TPP data.

claim: TOMM40 is a translocase located in the outer membrane of the mitochondria that has been implicated in tissue protective effects against late-onset Alzheimer disease.
source: TOMM40 is a translocase located in the outer membrane of the mitochondria that has been implicated in tissue protective effects against late-onset Alzheimer disease (Chiba-Falek et al., 2018) and COX6C is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, catalyzing the electron transfer from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chiba-Falek et al., 2018.

claim: COX6C is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, catalyzing the electron transfer from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen.
source: TOMM40 is a translocase located in the outer membrane of the mitochondria that has been implicated in tissue protective effects against late-onset Alzheimer disease (Chiba-Falek et al., 2018) and COX6C is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, catalyzing the electron transfer from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about COX6C function.

claim: Treatment with SNC80 (100 µM) suppressed OCR and ATP production relative to control levels within 1.5 hr in epithelial cells derived from intestine and liver without detectable cytotoxicity.
source: Treatment with SNC80 (100 µM) suppressed OCR and ATP production relative to control levels within 1.5 hr in epithelial cells derived from intestine and liver (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) without detectable cytotoxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a), indicating a decrease in cellular metabolism similar to Xenopus.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a and cytotoxicity data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: A reduction in creatine kinase activity was observed in both intestinal and liver epithelial cell types after SNC80 treatment.
source: Furthermore, we observed a reduction in creatine kinase activity in both epithelial cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), indicating a decrease in overall cell energy demand (Klepinina et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by creatine kinase activity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Reduction in creatine kinase activity indicates a decrease in overall cell energy demand.
source: Furthermore, we observed a reduction in creatine kinase activity in both epithelial cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), indicating a decrease in overall cell energy demand (Klepinina et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from creatine kinase activity data and citation to Klepinina et al., 2021.

claim: The Caco-2 cells exposed to SNC80 showed a dramatic increase in ECAR and glutamate production.
source: The Caco-2 cells exposed to SNC80 showed a dramatic increase in ECAR and glutamate production (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the cells activate compensatory mechanisms such as glycolysis and CRC pathway (Fendt et al., 2013; Posho et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR and glutamate data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The increase in ECAR and glutamate production in Caco-2 cells suggests that the cells activate compensatory mechanisms such as glycolysis and CRC pathway.
source: The Caco-2 cells exposed to SNC80 showed a dramatic increase in ECAR and glutamate production (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the cells activate compensatory mechanisms such as glycolysis and CRC pathway (Fendt et al., 2013; Posho et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ECAR and glutamate data and citations to Fendt et al., 2013; Posho et al., 1998.

claim: The Huh7 cells showed no change in ECAR nor glutamate after SNC80 treatment.
source: Unlike Caco-2, the Huh7 cells showed no change in ECAR nor glutamate (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b) after SNC80 treatment, suggesting that cells did not compensate mitochondrial impairment with increased glycolytic activity or CRC.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR and glutamate data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Huh7 cells did not compensate mitochondrial impairment with increased glycolytic activity or CRC after SNC80 treatment.
source: Unlike Caco-2, the Huh7 cells showed no change in ECAR nor glutamate (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b) after SNC80 treatment, suggesting that cells did not compensate mitochondrial impairment with increased glycolytic activity or CRC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ECAR and glutamate data.

claim: SNC80 must decrease total ATP production in Huh7 cells.
source: SNC80 must therefore decrease total ATP production, which was confirmed by detection of a significant drop in the ATP/ADP ratio within liver epithelial cells expressing a fluorescent reporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and confirmed by ATP/ADP ratio data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 2 hr of SNC80 treatment in HUVEC and LSEC reduced mitochondrial ATP production.
source: When looking at endothelial cells, 2 hr of SNC80 treatment in HUVEC and LSEC reduced mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating a decrease in mitochondrial activity and slowing of metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: 2 hr of SNC80 treatment in HUVEC and LSEC did not alter OCR.
source: When looking at endothelial cells, 2 hr of SNC80 treatment in HUVEC and LSEC reduced mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating a decrease in mitochondrial activity and slowing of metabolism. However, it did not alter OCR.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: HUVEC and LSEC showed no change in ECAR or glutamate after SNC80 treatment.
source: HUVEC and LSEC showed no change in ECAR or glutamate (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the cells are not compensating with additional glycolysis or CRC and that therefore the overall ATP production in the cell line is decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR and glutamate data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The overall ATP production in HUVEC and LSEC is decreased after SNC80 treatment.
source: HUVEC and LSEC showed no change in ECAR or glutamate (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the cells are not compensating with additional glycolysis or CRC and that therefore the overall ATP production in the cell line is decreased.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ECAR and glutamate data.

claim: All four human cell types showed significant decreases in mitochondrial metabolism in response to the biostasis inducer SNC80.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that all four human cell types showed significant decreases in mitochondrial metabolism in response to the biostasis inducer SNC80.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined results of all cell type experiments.

claim: Caco-2 cells were the only ones that activated compensatory pathways in response to the impaired mitochondrial respiration caused by SNC80.
source: However, Caco-2 cells were the only ones that activated compensatory pathways in response to the impaired mitochondrial respiration, while others just allowed for their energy balance to decrease significantly.
